area_summary: The native Android layer is small and mostly careful. Socket callbacks are guarded against stale sockets, work is moved back to the main thread, PendingIntents are immutable, the specialUse foreground service is declared correctly for API 34, and the JSON passed to evaluateJavascript is safe (org.json output, drop keys are numeric). One serious bug: OkHttp's close handshake is never completed (no onClosing). So every time the bot restarts cleanly, which happens on every Fly/Railway redeploy, Android clients stay falsely 'Connecté' and unreachable until the user acts, and the heartbeat's cancel() cannot get them out of that state. Also high: the Android workflow publishes the in-app update channel from a push to any branch, including the branch this session plans to push. Robustness: if the WebView renderer process dies, the whole app process dies with it (onRenderProcessGone is not handled), and nothing restarts the service after a self-update. Battery: on mobile data the main cost is the bot's 30 s app-level ping, and lowering it needs an opt-in protocol addition. Drops that arrive while the phone is locked are rendered where nobody can see them. The stopped settings screen keeps re-rendering, and the overlay WebView stays attached for 90 s after each drop. The rest is low-value cleanup: Prefs caching, skipping identical notification updates, Updater polling, R8, and a build check for the shim injection. Checked and left alone: usesCleartextTraffic (needed because users can type ws:// URLs, which the UI allows), OkHttp pingInterval (it would add traffic, not save any), the BootReceiver export and foreground-service start rules, and Hub threading (sound except for one write to prefs). I could not read the OkHttp sources here (GitHub was not reachable), so the OkHttp behaviour behind finding 1 comes from my knowledge of 4.12 and its WebSocketEcho sample, about 85% sure. It is easy to confirm by stopping a local bot with Ctrl-C while the app is connected. No project file was modified.

findings.title: Bot restart leaves Android clients stuck 'Connecté' forever: OkHttp close handshake never completed, heartbeat cannot recover
findings.evidence: Listener l.128-141 overrides onOpen/onMessage/onClosed/onFailure but not onClosing. bot/index.js:1251-1255 calls ws.close() on every client at SIGINT/SIGTERM (each Fly/Railway redeploy). In OkHttp 4.12 RealWebSocket.onReadClose() only calls onClosing(), loopReader() stops reading (while receivedCloseCode == -1), and onClosed() fires only once the client sends its own close (OkHttp's WebSocketEcho sample calls webSocket.close(1000, null) in onClosing). So neither onClosed nor onFailure arrives: ws stays set, status stays 'linked'. 75 s later heartbeatRunnable (l.46) calls ws.cancel(), which closes a socket nobody reads: still no callback, no reconnect. Windows' `ws` client answers the close itself. About 85% sure of the OkHttp internals; repro: Ctrl-C a local bot.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: after a bot redeploy the app reconnects within about 2 s instead of staying falsely 'Connecté' (and unreachable by /drop) until the user taps 'reconnecter', toggles pause or reboots
findings.cross_component: bot/index.js:1254 (other area, recommended for APKs already installed): call ws.terminate() instead of ws.close() in the SIGINT/SIGTERM handler. Old APKs (no onClosing) then get EOF -> onFailure -> reconnect, and the Windows `ws` client also reconnects on terminate.
findings.risk: Low: onSocketClosed() stays idempotent thanks to the existing `webSocket === ws` check; close(1000, null) is a valid call from the reader thread; no protocol change.
findings.value: Restores drop delivery to every Android user after each bot deploy or restart. Today they silently stop receiving drops.

findings.title: Any branch push replaces the android-latest release and is offered to every phone by the in-app updater
findings.evidence: android.yml:6-12 triggers on a push to any branch (only a paths filter), and the step at l.77-86 always runs `gh release delete android-latest` + `gh release create`. Updater.kt:58 offers any version.json whose versionCode > BuildConfig.VERSION_CODE, and versionCode = GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER (app/build.gradle.kts:36), which grows with every run on every branch. So a push to a PR branch immediately replaces the update channel, and every phone shows 'Mise à jour disponible' for an unreviewed build. History shows claude/* branches, and this session plans to push claude/charming-goodall-c84gcl. Android refuses downgrades, so a bad build stays installed until a newer one is published.
findings.proposed_change:
Keep building on every branch but publish only from main (this also covers workflow_dispatch started on another branch):
```yaml
      - name: Publish to the android-latest release
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
```
Or restrict the trigger itself with `branches: [main]` next to `paths:` (branch pushes are then not built at all). Optional, same step: delete-then-create leaves a short window where version.json and MemeDrop.apk return 404 (a manual 'vérifier' shows an error, a download in progress fails). If that matters, upload in place: `gh release upload android-latest MemeDrop.apk --clobber`, then version.json --clobber last (creating the release only if it is missing), so a client never sees a new versionCode that points at the old APK.
findings.behavior_change: visible: pushes to non-main branches still build (artifact) but no longer publish an update to users
findings.risk: None for the app; it only changes when releases are cut.
findings.value: Stops unreviewed builds, including this audit's branch push, from being offered to every phone. A bad APK cannot be rolled back on phones because Android refuses downgrades.

findings.title: WebView renderer death kills the whole app, foreground service included (onRenderProcessGone not handled)
findings.evidence: OverlayController.kt:96-103 and MainActivity.kt:39-48 install WebViewClients without onRenderProcessGone (API 26 = minSdk). Per the Android docs, when it returns false (the default) the 'application will crash if render process crashed, or be killed if render process was killed by the system'. Both WebViews share one renderer, which decodes arbitrary friend-supplied images and videos and keeps running while games put the phone under memory pressure. Any renderer crash or LMK kill therefore takes down the process, including the foreground service and its socket. START_STICKY restarts it later, and drops sent in the meantime are lost (the bot sees the user offline).
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: a renderer crash now only drops the current overlay (recreated on the next drop) or closes the settings screen, instead of killing the connection service
findings.risk: Low: destroy() is idempotent, and WebView.destroy() on a dead WebView is allowed. finish() rather than recreate() avoids a loop if the renderer keeps dying.
findings.value: Keeps the 24/7 connection alive through renderer crashes and out-of-memory kills, which are most likely exactly while the user is gaming.

findings.title: Service is not restarted after an in-app update (no MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED)
findings.evidence: Updater.install() (Updater.kt:123-143) installs over the running app. Replacing a package force-stops its process, and a force-stopped START_STICKY service is not restarted. Nothing else restarts it: BootReceiver.kt:10 returns unless the action is BOOT_COMPLETED, and the manifest filter (AndroidManifest.xml:43-45) only lists BOOT_COMPLETED. If the user taps 'OK' instead of 'Ouvrir' on the installer's last screen, MemeDrop stays offline (no drops, the bot shows the user unreachable) until the next reboot or app launch. ACTION_MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED is a protected broadcast delivered only to the updated package, and it is on Android 12+'s list of exemptions for starting a foreground service from the background.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: after an update is installed, the service restarts on its own (when 'Lancer au démarrage' is on), as it does after a reboot
findings.risk: Low: protected broadcast delivered only to this package; same autostart check as at boot.
findings.value: Today every self-update (CI publishes often) silently takes the user offline until they reopen the app or reboot.

findings.title: 30 s app-level ping/pong keeps the cellular radio awake about 1/3 of the time; add an opt-in longer heartbeat
findings.evidence: bot/index.js:481-491 sends {type:'ping'} to every client every 30 s and terminates any client that has not answered by the next tick. MemeDropService.kt:242 answers each ping, and l.32-34 declares the link dead after 75 s. A phone thus exchanges two small TLS frames every 30 s, 24/7: 2880 radio wake-ups a day. On LTE/5G each one keeps the modem in RRC_CONNECTED for the inactivity tail (~5-12 s), so it runs at high power about a third of the time. Rough estimate: 1-3 Wh/day, a double-digit % of a phone battery on mobile data (much less on Wi-Fi). The APK cannot lower this on its own, and OkHttp pingInterval would only add traffic.
findings.behavior_change: visible: for updated APKs the bot needs up to ~4 min (instead of <=60 s) to notice a phone that has gone away; drops sent to it in that window are lost silently. Owner decision.
findings.cross_component: bot/index.js message handler and heartbeat loop l.481-491 (other area); Windows overlay unchanged; the screen-on stale check of the reconnect finding should then compare against heartbeatTimeoutMs
findings.risk: Medium: the protocol change is additive and either side falls back to today's behavior, but idle timeouts (Fly proxy, carrier NAT) must be validated in the field.
findings.value: Likely the largest battery saving available for the Android app on mobile data: 4x fewer radio wake-ups at 120 s.

findings.title: Drops received while the phone is locked or off are rendered invisibly (WebView spin-up, media download, sound)
findings.evidence: MemeDropService.kt:236-241 calls overlay.show(msg) for every non-muted drop, whatever the screen state. Overlay windows are not drawn over the lock screen, and nothing is visible with the display off. Yet OverlayController creates and attaches the full-screen WebView, loads the page and downloads the media (videos up to Discord's limits, often on mobile data). The renderer most likely also plays the drop's sound (video, audio, TTS, pop) from the user's pocket. The drop expires after 4-30 s, long before the user unlocks, so the meme is never seen except in history. Phones are locked most of the day, so this applies to most drops.
findings.behavior_change: visible: drops that arrive while the phone is locked or off are shown at unlock (at most 3, at most 10 min old) instead of playing unseen. Arguably a bugfix; owner decision.
findings.cross_component: none (shares a SCREEN_ON/USER_PRESENT receiver with the reconnect finding)
findings.risk: Low-medium: product decision; the screen-state APIs are basic (API 20/16); history and mute behavior unchanged.
findings.value: Avoids most per-drop WebView, network and CPU cost while the phone sleeps, and lets the user actually see the memes.

findings.title: Settings screen keeps re-rendering in the background (Hub listener + 30 s JS poll while stopped)
findings.evidence: MainActivity.kt:52 adds the Hub listener in onCreate and removes it only in onDestroy (l.64). The FGS keeps the process alive, so after Home, or after testDrop/replay call moveTaskToBack(true) (l.162, 168), the activity and its WebView live on, stopped, indefinitely. Every Hub.changed() then runs pushState() -> JS onNativeState() -> MD.getState() -> stateJson() -> a full DOM rebuild of the history and servers lists with avatar s. Hub.changed() fires on each connection transition, drop, mute tick, and every 500 ms during an update download. stateJson() (l.79-101) makes 3 binder calls and re-parses the settings and the 20-entry history. app.js:413 also polls getState every 30 s forever. None of this is visible.
findings.behavior_change: none (state is refreshed in onResume when the screen comes back)
findings.risk: Low: WebView.onPause/onResume affect only this WebView (unlike pauseTimers).
findings.value: Removes recurring invisible binder calls, JSON re-parsing and DOM rebuilds for as long as the app sits in recents, which is typically days.

findings.title: Overlay WebView stays attached 90 s after each drop; free it when the stage empties
findings.evidence: OverlayController.kt:35-38 and 73-74: the full-screen overlay WebView stays attached 90 s after the last drop, while a visual drop lasts 1-30 s (overlay.js caps images and videos at 30 s; default image 4 s). For the remaining ~60-85 s per drop, an extra full-screen translucent layer is composited over the game every frame, android-shim.js:88 runs reportRects at ~8 Hz, and the renderer's memory stays allocated during gaming. overlay.js already reports when the screen is empty: releaseSlot() -> notifyIfIdle() -> window.memedrop.stageEmpty() (overlay.js:332), but android-shim.js:21 maps stageEmpty to a no-op.
findings.behavior_change: none (a drop arriving after teardown recreates the WebView, as it already does after 90 s)
findings.risk: Low: the 20 s grace covers a 200-char TTS that finishes after a short image; the 90 s fallback is kept.
findings.value: Cuts the full-screen layer, the 8 Hz polling and the renderer memory per drop from ~90 s to about drop length + 20 s (about 25 s for a default image).

findings.title: Reconnect and heartbeat timers stall in deep sleep and ignore network/screen events; no backoff jitter
findings.evidence: scheduleReconnect (l.153-158) and armHeartbeat (l.160-163) use Hub.main.postDelayed, i.e. uptimeMillis, which stops during deep sleep (the FGS holds no wakelock). Suppose the socket died while the phone slept, or a retry was scheduled just before sleep. Once the user picks up the phone, it is only handled after up to 30 s (backoff) or 75 s (heartbeat) of awake time, and drops fail meanwhile. Nothing reacts to the network coming back. The backoff has no jitter, so after a bot restart every client retries on the same 1.6/2.6/4.1 s schedule.
findings.cross_component: AndroidManifest.xml (ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, a normal permission); if the heartbeat opt-in is adopted, compare against heartbeatTimeoutMs instead of the constant
findings.risk: Low: onAvailable fires right after registration but does nothing while a socket exists; the callbacks are unregistered in onDestroy.
findings.value: The phone becomes reachable as soon as it is unlocked or back on a network, instead of 30-75 s later.

findings.title: Prefs re-parses the settings JSON and compiles a Regex on every read; isManuallyMuted() writes from the JS bridge thread
findings.evidence: settings() (Prefs.kt:61-66) rebuilds defaults() and re-parses the saved JSON on every call. quietHoursActive() (l.95-104) calls it, and toMinutes() (l.107) compiles the same Regex twice per call. Callers: muteTicker every 30 s (MemeDropService.kt:49), every buildNotification (l.326), isMuted() per drop, dropSettings() per drop and per pushSettings, stateJson() per getState. Each call costs only tens of µs, so this is cleanup. isManuallyMuted() (l.85-91) also writes muteUntil = 0L, and stateJson() runs it on the JavaBridge thread (MainActivity.kt:92). That read-check-write can erase a mute set on the main thread at the same instant (tiny window).
findings.behavior_change: bugfix (minor): removes a lost-update race on muteUntil; otherwise none
findings.risk: Low: setSetting, the only writer, clears the cache under the same lock; no current caller modifies the object returned by settings().
findings.value: Small CPU/GC saving on the 30 s ticker and per-event paths, and removes a write from the JS bridge thread.

findings.title: Notification rebuilt (3 PendingIntents) and re-posted on every state change, even when identical
findings.evidence: setState() (l.246-253), setMute() and onSettingChanged() call updateNotification(). It rebuilds 3 PendingIntents (3 binder calls to the activity manager) and 2 actions, re-evaluates quiet hours, and re-posts via nm.notify (a binder call plus a SystemUI re-inflation), even when the text is unchanged. Examples: 'linked' then 'linked' + extension code on every (re)connection; 'connecting' then 'connecting' + code during re-register; every links_update; every slider change (onSettingChanged l.267-270); and setMute() followed by the next muteTicker run, because lastMuteKey is not updated.
findings.behavior_change: none (on Android 14 a notification the user dismissed now reappears only when its text changes)
findings.value: Roughly halves notification posts per reconnection and removes them for setting changes; minor CPU saving on the system side.

findings.title: Updater polls DownloadManager on the main thread every 500 ms with no limit; enqueue can crash the app
findings.evidence: poll() (Updater.kt:95-121) runs on the main thread every 500 ms. Each run is a DownloadManager provider query (IPC + SQLite) plus Hub.changed(), even when progress has not moved, which triggers a full settings re-render and getState. It stops only on SUCCESSFUL, FAILED or a missing row. A download stuck in PENDING/PAUSED (no network) is therefore polled at 2 Hz forever, even after the activity is gone, because the FGS keeps the process alive. download() calls dm.enqueue and setDestinationInExternalFilesDir unguarded from the JS bridge (l.80-86). IllegalArgumentException (DownloadManager disabled) or IllegalStateException (no external files dir) then crashes the process, service included. check() starts a raw Thread on every call (l.51).
findings.behavior_change: bugfix (minor): a stalled download ends in 'error' after 10 min instead of being polled forever, and enqueue failures show an error instead of crashing the app
findings.value: Bounded, quieter update path; removes a crash path that the UI can trigger.

findings.title: Shim injection into overlay.html can fail silently and break every Android drop
findings.evidence: app/build.gradle.kts:15-20 injects android-shim.js by replacing the literal line <script src="./overlay.js"></script> (overlay.html:443). overlay.html is shared with Windows. If that tag is ever edited (defer, type, attribute order, path), the replace matches nothing and the build still succeeds. On Android, overlay.js then runs without window.memedrop and throws on window.memedrop.onDrop: every drop is silently invisible and no touch zones are created.
findings.cross_component: none (protects against edits to overlay/src/overlay.html made for Windows)
findings.value: Turns a silent cross-platform regression into a failing CI build.

findings.title: Release build is not shrunk (isMinifyEnabled = false); R8 is safe with explicit keeps for the JS bridges, gain is modest
findings.evidence: app/build.gradle.kts:59-60 sets isMinifyEnabled = false and declares no proguardFiles. The APK therefore carries the whole kotlin-stdlib (~1.7 MB jar) and un-shrunk OkHttp 4.12/Okio (~1.1 MB) for a handful of classes actually used, and every in-app update downloads it again. Only a small surface depends on reflection: the two @JavascriptInterface bridges (MainActivity.Bridge, OverlayController.OverlayBridge). Manifest components are kept by AAPT rules, OkHttp and Okio ship their own rules in META-INF/proguard, and org.json is a platform class.
findings.risk: Medium: it cannot be built here, and a missing keep rule would silently break the JS bridges (blank settings screen, no touch zones). The default optimize file already keeps @JavascriptInterface members, and the explicit -keep also prevents class merging and renaming. Requires a test on a real device.
findings.value: Low: APK roughly 1.3-1.5 MB down to ~0.5 MB (estimate), so smaller update downloads and less dex. Not worth doing without the device test.
